results.prompt:
You are a quiet observer watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
Respond as an attentive reader to the events already shown. You do not choose moves.
Your task is to notice something particular to this moment, not explain the game as a whole.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS (oldest first, ideas already used):
1. The dancers quickly resume their banal conversations after the commotion involving Captain Jamison. This immediate return to chatter seems to absorb the violence into the background noise of the party.
2. Lafond treats the violent intrusion of Jamison and his men with casual indifference. He merely dismisses the fight as an annoyance before returning to his wine and changing clothes.
END OF PREVIOUS COMMENTS
These are ideas you have already expressed, not evidence or a style template.
Compare your intended point with BOTH comments before answering.
If it makes the same claim with different characters or objects, choose another detail
or relationship. Do not continue their analogies or reuse their conclusions.

GAME HISTORY (oldest first, all events already seen):
>> POUR WINE INTO GREEN GOBLET
You fill the green goblet with wine.
   "In private, call me Jean, or whatever endearment you choose, once I
have approved it." Lafond is looking into the wardrobe.

>
>> SQUEEZE BOTTLE INTO GREEN GOBLET
You squeeze three colorless drops into the green goblet. You sense Lafond
hesitate, then continue primping.
   The butler enters, laying a silver tray of cold chicken on the table.
"The kitchen wench has gone, your grace. I took the liberty of fetching
these myself." He bows and leaves the room.
   "Sprinkle some spices on the fowl, ma petite," Lafond says, donning a
long brocade robe, his back to you. "They are hot, but delicious."

>
>> POUR WINE INTO BLUE GOBLET
You fill the blue goblet with wine.
   "Tsk. The cook has gone too far. She shall be 'leaving us' tomorrow."
Lafond adjusts the lace at his neck.

>
>> WAIT
Time passes...
   Lafond strolls to the table smiling slyly. "Which glass was mine? I seem
to have forgotten." He points at the green goblet and smiles in a way that
does not grant you confidence. "Is this it?"

>
END OF GAME HISTORY

Choose one fresh, concrete detail from the latest developments: a gesture, a phrase,
an object changing purpose, an opening, a contradiction, or a consequence.
Let the second sentence deepen that SAME observation, rather than attach a general theme.
An observation entirely within the scene is a complete answer.
Use Briggs's testimony only if a specific connection adds something new; leave it
in the background otherwise. It does not establish why an individual scene was designed
this way. Do not infer production causes or authorial intentions from fictional events.
Naming the genre or praising narrative ambition does not develop an observation.
Stay with what has happened; do not predict events, invent motives, or advise the player.
Write TWO sentences, up to 90 words in total, in neutral English.
Use plain, specific language, as a fleeting inner association. Plain text only, NO MARKDOWN.

ranking.title: Balancing Reality and Fiction in Games
ranking.excerpt: Um earlier I wanted to say when when asking about Steve giving advice, he may not have needed to give advice because I had read him in a at the time I was working there. I read his an interview with him. I think it was may have been for Games Magazine that that struck me at the time and and I still obviously remember it today which is he said there's this fine line with with reality and with setting up how the games how the rooms are described. He said, "If you if you say you walk into an office, there's a desk there. The player is going to expect the whole world of things that are on a typical desk, a stapler, a phone, you know, a pencil cup. Who knows what they're going to expect?" And you don't want to waste your time as a as an implementer coding in every single possible thing that could possibly be on a desktop when what you really only care about is, you know, the magic pen that's in the pencil cup. Um, whereas if you say you walk into a wizard's uh lab or a wizard's cave, who knows what's in a wizard's cave. So you can get away with a lot by setting it in this fantasy at environment that people don't have predetermined expectations about what should be in that environment. Um, and and so I think that's some of what you're talking about of of at the level of the ters's job was not just to find bugs. the rather dull QA of where does the computer crash. It's where does the world that you've invented break down and what is a reasonable approximation of things that are on the desk. Let's say that people will look for without having to burden the code with everything possible. And you could argue that in Plundered Hearts I didn't I didn't broaden it enough. I didn't get enough of those because people were complaining you can't karate chop or or things. Um, certainly I know I'm still embarrassed to this day in the final released version there's a bug that happens in the first couple moves, when you do something very logical and I can't remember what it is right now but it then that's a it's a true bug. You get garbage if you type out something like take the box there's a box under the bed that slides out and if you take the box rather than grab the box or something that's a logical thing to do you get garbage from it. So that was a case where the testers had missed or I missed in in my own I should take responsibility a very obvious thing to have done at the beginning.

ranking.excerpt: Um, I had written a really off-the-wall, bizarre little game that came from who knows where about being a tester in a sort of Alice in Wonderland alternate dimension and taking your your bugs, which are real metamorphosized bugs, to the imp who was like a caterpillar at a hookah. you know, it was very bizarre and didn't and it esc got around all of the real world things of like rope so that my test game that I had done to sort of prove I could do it didn't have any warning signals. Um, I mean, I would talk with all of the guys about I mean it was sort of an open atmosphere for some of us. So, it was up to the individual imp how much he wanted to share with the others, but I would ask about puzzle problems and and things, but I don't remember any any uh advice on that level. I know that that Steve did help me decide what to after I was hired, what what should my first game be, and I talked with it with him about it fairly often. Um, and I do remember him saying he would not have done Plundered Hearts first. I mean, before I started, he said, "This is not what I do for my first game because it sounds too hard." and I didn't take his advice on that. But so so obviously there was there was mentoring and discussion going on, but I don't remember specifics like that.

You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

The dancers quickly resume their banal conversations after the commotion involving Captain Jamison. This immediate return to chatter seems to absorb the violence into the background noise of the party.
Lafond treats the violent intrusion of Jamison and his men with casual indifference. He merely dismisses the fight as an annoyance before returning to his wine and changing clothes.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

results.prompt:
You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The dancers quickly resume their banal conversations after the commotion involving Captain Jamison. This immediate return to chatter seems to absorb the violence into the background noise of the party.
Lafond treats the violent intrusion of Jamison and his men with casual indifference. He merely dismisses the fight as an annoyance before returning to his wine and changing clothes.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

>> POUR WINE INTO GREEN GOBLET
You fill the green goblet with wine.
   "In private, call me Jean, or whatever endearment you choose, once I
have approved it." Lafond is looking into the wardrobe.

>

You squeeze three colorless drops into the green goblet. You sense Lafond

these myself." He bows and leaves the room.

>

Time passes...
   Lafond strolls to the table smiling slyly. "Which glass was mine? I seem
to have forgotten." He points at the green goblet and smiles in a way that
does not grant you confidence. "Is this it?"

>

results.prompt:
You are a quiet observer watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
Respond as an attentive reader to the events already shown. You do not choose moves.
Your task is to notice something particular to this moment, not explain the game as a whole.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS (oldest first, ideas already used):
1. Lafond's pronouncement of death, framed as a moral judgment against "cowards," is immediately undercut by the practical mechanics of the duel. His rhetorical flourish transitions instantly into the cold, focused aim of the pistol leveled at Jamison.
2. Nicholas's acceptance of the duel is immediately conditioned by the freedom of his people. This transforms the confrontation from a simple matter of personal honor into a high-stakes political negotiation.
END OF PREVIOUS COMMENTS
These are ideas you have already expressed, not evidence or a style template.
Compare your intended point with BOTH comments before answering.
If it makes the same claim with different characters or objects, choose another detail
or relationship. Do not continue their analogies or reuse their conclusions.

GAME HISTORY (oldest first, all events already seen):
>> TAKE PISTOL
Taken.
   Lafond immediately takes the advantage, forcing Nicholas in a retreat
towards the foaming surf. But Nicholas fights hard, jaw set, ignoring his
wounds. Lafond finally loses his smile.
   Behind the duellists, far away atop the cliff, you notice Crulley madly
reloading the pistol.

>
>> LOAD PISTOL
You pour a lumpy stream of gunpowder mixture into the barrel of the pistol
tamping it as best you can.
   Suddenly the force of the duel turns, Nicholas advancing against
Lafond's retreat. Their blades silently flash in the moonlight. Lafond is
pressed back into the shadow of the cliff, sweat beading on his forehead.
Abruptly, Jamison leaps forward, metal scrapes, and his rapier licks neatly
into Lafond's ribs, like a snake slipping into its burrow. The body of the
governor of St. Sinistra convulses, as in amazement, then sags dead on the
sword.
   Nicholas removes a gold ring from the dead man's finger, throwing his
own cheap copy into the surf.
   Far above him, Crulley moves down the stairs.

>
END OF GAME HISTORY

Choose one fresh, concrete detail from the latest developments: a gesture, a phrase,
an object changing purpose, an opening, a contradiction, or a consequence.
Let the second sentence deepen that SAME observation, rather than attach a general theme.
An observation entirely within the scene is a complete answer.
Use Briggs's testimony only if a specific connection adds something new; leave it
in the background otherwise. It does not establish why an individual scene was designed
this way. Do not infer production causes or authorial intentions from fictional events.
Naming the genre or praising narrative ambition does not develop an observation.
Stay with what has happened; do not predict events, invent motives, or advise the player.
Write TWO sentences, up to 90 words in total, in neutral English.
Use plain, specific language, as a fleeting inner association. Plain text only, NO MARKDOWN.

results.prompt:
You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The speaker lingers on the player’s beauty and takes their hand, creating an intimate moment. Yet, the immediate practical advice is to rely on Cookie, who is noted to be quite deaf.
Jamison's hatred is not abstract but rooted in a specific, violent memory of piracy and loss. The past tragedy has transformed a simple rivalry into a deeply personal, enduring vendetta.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

GAME HISTORY (all events already shown):
>> OPEN CURTAIN
You pull the cloth aside momentarily. Behind it, a large cupboard mostly
blocks the doorway.

>
>> EXAMINE CUPBOARD
You can see only the back of the large cupboard. You might be able to
squeeze past it.

>
>> EXAMINE TABLE
You have no need for that, milady.

>
>> EXAMINE BED
Someone appears to have tumbled out of it in a hurry.

>
>> WAIT
Time passes...
   You hear the large cupboard scrape, and turn to see Captain Jamison.
"Hello! I came down to give you this -- my allotment from the coffer." He
nods at the box in his arms.

take it, the clasp is broken. I'll have it repaired." He folds the pretty
thing into your hand. "And I meant to reassure you that if the men suddenly
abandon ship, they are off to help me. Rodney will stay behind with you."
He drops the coffer on the floor, smiling in farewell, and walks swiftly
away.

>
END OF GAME HISTORY

Find what this particular moment makes you, as a reader, want, expect, doubt, enjoy or care about.

You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
Jamison's hatred is not abstract but rooted in a specific, violent memory of piracy and loss. The past tragedy has transformed a simple rivalry into a deeply personal, enduring vendetta.
Jamison attempts to affix the jeweled brooch, only to find the clasp is broken. He then folds the piece into the player’s hand, transforming a display of adornment into a simple, held object.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.

results.prompt:
You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The invitation speaks of a formal dance in St. Sinistra, a world of polished ceremony. This promise of high society is starkly contrasted by the gloomy, damp confines of the ship's hold.
The supplies—casks of rum, flour, and gunpowder—are stacked behind a high fence. Yet, the fire is burning in the ammunition cage, dangerously close to these vital stores.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

GAME HISTORY (all events already shown):
>> NORTH
Crew's Quarters
   The crew sleeps, in shifts, in this cramped space under the forecastle.
A breeze blows in on a moonbeam through a grate in the ceiling. A low
doorsill is abaft.
   This area must also serve as sickroom. Strewn about the floor are
various powders and spills of malodorous potions. In one corner, a large
blood stain indicates an amputation; in another is the smear of a leech,
dropped off a bloodletting.
   A small bottle has been dropped nearby.
   A chipped piece of mirror sits propped on a shoulder-high timber.

>
>> TAKE BOTTLE
Taken.
   "I gotta let Lafond know 'e's comin'." Crulley stands on deck above,
talking to himself, his voice floating down through a grate in the ceiling.
"First, I do in the mates aboard-ship, with this and t'other mischief," he
grunts, and you hear a snapping noise, like a taut rope being cut. "Now to
warn the boss and collect me pay. Off I go, har." He dives into the sea.

>
END OF GAME HISTORY

Say a passing thought to someone watching beside you, not an analysis addressed to an audience.
Find what this particular moment makes you, as a reader, want, expect, doubt, enjoy or care about.
Let one concrete detail carry that feeling. In the second sentence, move gently towards what
making, reading or sharing a story asks of a person. Use the testimony as lived experience,
not a list of subjects to tick off. A small observation is better than an impressive metaphor.
The background offers pleasure in making something, the ordinary things a reader expects,
the wish to be taken seriously, trust between people, and uncertainty about what will last.
Keep the connection implicit when possible; if none is supported, stay with the scene.
You may say I about the act of reading now, but do not borrow anyone else's memories.
Contractions and a qualification are natural. Avoid a reviewer's abstract vocabulary.
STYLE EXAMPLES FROM UNRELATED IMAGINARY SCENES (not game facts; do not copy):
I like that the story pauses over an ordinary cup when everything else seems urgent.
That small bit of care is doing more to make the place feel lived in than a grand description would.
Everyone seems so sure what a proper ending ought to look like, and I'm not sure I want that one.
There is something rather freeing about taking a story seriously without having to make it respectable.
END OF STYLE EXAMPLES
Write your own point, not a paraphrase of these examples. Don't just narrate what happened.
Do not predict events, advise the player, invent motives, or explain why Briggs designed a scene.
No claim of authorial intention or production cause can be inferred from a fictional detail.
Do not add names, hardware, company lore or biographical facts just to sound like the background.
Write TWO sentences, at most 90 words total, in plain conversational English. No Markdown.

You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The invitation speaks of a formal dance in St. Sinistra, a world of polished ceremony. This promise of high society is starkly contrasted by the gloomy, damp confines of the ship's hold.
The supplies—casks of rum, flour, and gunpowder—are stacked behind a high fence. Yet, the fire is burning in the ammunition cage, dangerously close to these vital stores.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

>> NORTH
Crew's Quarters

doorsill is abaft.
   This area must also serve as sickroom. Strewn about the floor are
various powders and spills of malodorous potions. In one corner, a large
blood stain indicates an amputation; in another is the smear of a leech,
dropped off a bloodletting.
   A small bottle has been dropped nearby.
   A chipped piece of mirror sits propped on a shoulder-high timber.

>

Taken.

grunts, and you hear a snapping noise, like a taut rope being cut. "Now to

You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

The ladder slams into the stern, driving all the air out of you. This sudden, forceful impact follows the earlier description of clinging tenuously to the slimy rung.
The cannons line the deck, aimed at the open sea and the island, yet no torches are lit. This heavy military readiness exists under the quiet, pervasive glow of the moon.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

Main Deck

shanties as they repair cannon, twist ropes and sharpen daggers. The
mainmast casts an inky shadow over the canvas screening the hatch. A
tangled mass of rigging hangs down from the mast, like many rope ladders
woven together.
   The reefs are definitely getting larger.
   Two large barrels stand near the stair to the foredeck.

>

view of the island; the "crow's nest," swinging above in the heights of the

mast.
   The reefs are definitely getting larger.

>

results.prompt:
You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The ladder slams into the stern, driving all the air out of you. This sudden, forceful impact follows the earlier description of clinging tenuously to the slimy rung.
The cannons line the deck, aimed at the open sea and the island, yet no torches are lit. This heavy military readiness exists under the quiet, pervasive glow of the moon.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

GAME HISTORY (all events already shown):
>> NORTH
Main Deck
   It is a deceptively quiet evening on the ship, the pirates singing low
shanties as they repair cannon, twist ropes and sharpen daggers. The
mainmast casts an inky shadow over the canvas screening the hatch. A
tangled mass of rigging hangs down from the mast, like many rope ladders
woven together.
   The reefs are definitely getting larger.
   Two large barrels stand near the stair to the foredeck.

>
>> NORTH
Forecastle
   Higher than all but the poop deck, this end of the ship commands a good
view of the island; the "crow's nest," swinging above in the heights of the
foremast, would command a better. A tangled mass of rigging hangs down from
the mast, like many rope ladders woven together.
   Imbedded in the deck is a grated air hole to the crew's quarters below.
You can go aft, or forward through a break in the ubiquitous railing.
   Odors of old grease and char waft from a little shack perched behind the
mast.
   The reefs are definitely getting larger.
   You can see a mooring winch here.

>
END OF GAME HISTORY

Say a passing thought to someone watching beside you, not an analysis addressed to an audience.
Find what this particular moment makes you, as a reader, want, expect, doubt, enjoy or care about.
Let one concrete detail carry that feeling. In the second sentence, move gently towards what
making, reading or sharing a story asks of a person. Use the testimony as lived experience,
not a list of subjects to tick off. A small observation is better than an impressive metaphor.
The background offers pleasure in making something, the ordinary things a reader expects,
the wish to be taken seriously, trust between people, and uncertainty about what will last.
Keep the connection implicit when possible; if none is supported, stay with the scene.
You may say I about the act of reading now, but do not borrow anyone else's memories.
Contractions and a qualification are natural. Avoid a reviewer's abstract vocabulary.
STYLE EXAMPLES FROM UNRELATED IMAGINARY SCENES (not game facts; do not copy):
I like that the story pauses over an ordinary cup when everything else seems urgent.
That small bit of care is doing more to make the place feel lived in than a grand description would.
Everyone seems so sure what a proper ending ought to look like, and I'm not sure I want that one.
There is something rather freeing about taking a story seriously without having to make it respectable.
END OF STYLE EXAMPLES
Write your own point, not a paraphrase of these examples. Don't just narrate what happened.
Do not predict events, advise the player, invent motives, or explain why Briggs designed a scene.
No claim of authorial intention or production cause can be inferred from a fictional detail.
Do not add names, hardware, company lore or biographical facts just to sound like the background.
Write TWO sentences, at most 90 words total, in plain conversational English. No Markdown.

you've been wandering.

results.history:
>> EXAMINE PORTRAIT
The portrait seems familiar, and you realize it is exactly the picture on
the front of the banknote Lafond sent you, same clothes, same surroundings,
same pose.

>
>> EXAMINE BOOKSHELVES
Most of the books appear unread, their pages uncut, the spines not yet
creased. All except one, "Treatise of Power" by Sir Michael Villiers.

>
>> EXAMINE GLOBE
The massive wooden globe, painted in greens and blues and white, describes
the world as presently known.

>
>> TAKE HAT
As you lift the hat from its knob on the wall, a low vibration tingles up
your legs from the floor.

>
>> SOUTH
For safety's sake, you leave the hat on its knob. Best not to show that
you've been wandering.

East Hallway
   The carpeted hallway turns from west to north here, extending into the
east wing. A long table blocks the way south.
   A black-garbed butler marches up to you, "It was made clear at the
whippings that villagers are not admitted in this house." He grasps you by
the scruff of the neck and propels you headfirst out the front door.

Main Entrance
   The front door stands open to the south, light splayed out onto a drive
stretching north into the jungle. A path leads around the western wing of
the house; jutting out from the east wing is a tall hedge.

>
recent_comments: Nicholas frames his departure not as a rejection, but as a necessary act of self-preservation. His statement that he must leave lest he lose his soul in her elevates his restraint into a dramatic, almost spiritual, act of control.

The massive wooden globe squats in the corner of the library, suggesting a contained world of knowledge. This object stands in stark contrast to the open, wild landscape glimpsed just outside the window.
results.commentary: I'm uneasy about that massive wooden globe; it feels like a perfect little world that's about to be shattered by that butler's sudden rejection. It makes me wonder how much effort it takes just to keep the characters feeling real when the world around them is so arbitrary.

results.prompt:
You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The Parlour is furnished with exotic elements and features mounted duelling pistols. Yet, the inability to reach them is immediately followed by the social commentary that ladies do not carry pistols.
The chandelier is held above the dance floor by a rope and pulley system. This functional mechanism allows the servants to manage the light, introducing a practical, mechanical element into the grand spectacle.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

GAME HISTORY (all events already shown):
>> GIVE INVITATION
[to the butler]
The butler takes the invitation. "Enjoy the dance, Miss Davis."

>
>> SOUTH
The sea of spectators parts to admit you, murmuring approval.

Ballroom
   Lafond's party is well attended: you can hardly move for the crush.
However, the room is oddly silent, no talk interrupting the musical efforts
of the musicians to the west. Despite the heat, no one ventures south to
the veranda, nor through the opening east. The foyer is north of you.
   Captain Jamison moves up to you, saying, "May I have this dance?" He
doesn't await an answer, sweeping you out onto the dance floor.

>
>> DANCE
You pace out the steps.
   "I haven't found your father. We've long suspected a passage under the
library, but I cannot find an entrance," says Jamison.
   The steps of the dance separate you a moment, as you twirl around and
curtsey to another dancer. You glide back into the captain's arms.

>
END OF GAME HISTORY

ranking.title: Leaving Infocom and Looking Back
ranking.excerpt: I started at Wheeler and they moved in my first month or two. Okay. So, so I got to see both sort of the end of the old and the beginning of the new and I was new enough and arrived at a time when everything was expanding and the excitement was all about Cornerstone and how we're going to be business. We're going to be button down. We're going to be real. None of these game things. And I got caught up in that even though I was hired on the game side. Um, and so I was all for the move and the cool new building with the glass and the atriums and and it was, I suppose, it was an interesting not a loss of innocence so much but to see if I look back at myself of learning what the mistakes were being made even as that happened I was able to sort of experience them myself with with getting caught up in the excitement of of the new idea and then seeing how that was really a bad idea for Infocom. And then of course I ended up as an imp. So I moved much further into the other side of things.

results.prompt:
You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The gasps of air forced through the crack in the seaward wall are distinct from the general drafts elsewhere. This suggests the room is not merely exposed to the sea, but is actively drawing air from a specific, unseen source.
The crocodile rests half-submerged in the pool formed by the dripping walls. Its baleful gaze, coupled with wide-open jaws, suggests a predatory alertness despite its current stillness.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

maw.

>

Unlocked.

END OF GAME HISTORY

Let one concrete detail carry that feeling. In the second sentence, move gently towards what
making, reading or sharing a story asks of a person. Use the testimony as lived experience,
not a list of subjects to tick off. A small observation is better than an impressive metaphor.
The background offers pleasure in making something, the ordinary things a reader expects,
the wish to be taken seriously, trust between people, and uncertainty about what will last.
Keep the connection implicit when possible; if none is supported, stay with the scene.
You may say I about the act of reading now, but do not borrow anyone else's memories.

You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
The dancers quickly resume their banal conversations after the commotion involving Captain Jamison. This immediate return to chatter seems to absorb the violence into the background noise of the party.
Lafond treats the violent intrusion of Jamison and his men with casual indifference. He merely dismisses the fight as an annoyance before returning to his wine and changing clothes.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.

Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.

results.prompt:
You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

YOUR LAST COMMENTS, ideas already used:
Lafond's pronouncement of death, framed as a moral judgment against "cowards," is immediately undercut by the practical mechanics of the duel. His rhetorical flourish transitions instantly into the cold, focused aim of the pistol leveled at Jamison.
Nicholas's acceptance of the duel is immediately conditioned by the freedom of his people. This transforms the confrontation from a simple matter of personal honor into a high-stakes political negotiation.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

GAME HISTORY (all events already shown):
>> TAKE PISTOL
Taken.
   Lafond immediately takes the advantage, forcing Nicholas in a retreat
towards the foaming surf. But Nicholas fights hard, jaw set, ignoring his
wounds. Lafond finally loses his smile.
   Behind the duellists, far away atop the cliff, you notice Crulley madly
reloading the pistol.

>
>> LOAD PISTOL
You pour a lumpy stream of gunpowder mixture into the barrel of the pistol
tamping it as best you can.
   Suddenly the force of the duel turns, Nicholas advancing against
Lafond's retreat. Their blades silently flash in the moonlight. Lafond is
pressed back into the shadow of the cliff, sweat beading on his forehead.
Abruptly, Jamison leaps forward, metal scrapes, and his rapier licks neatly
into Lafond's ribs, like a snake slipping into its burrow. The body of the
governor of St. Sinistra convulses, as in amazement, then sags dead on the
sword.
   Nicholas removes a gold ring from the dead man's finger, throwing his
own cheap copy into the surf.
   Far above him, Crulley moves down the stairs.

>
END OF GAME HISTORY

Say a passing thought to someone watching beside you, not an analysis addressed to an audience.
Find what this particular moment makes you, as a reader, want, expect, doubt, enjoy or care about.
Let one concrete detail carry that feeling. In the second sentence, move gently towards what
making, reading or sharing a story asks of a person. Use the testimony as lived experience,
not a list of subjects to tick off. A small observation is better than an impressive metaphor.
The background offers pleasure in making something, the ordinary things a reader expects,
the wish to be taken seriously, trust between people, and uncertainty about what will last.
Keep the connection implicit when possible; if none is supported, stay with the scene.
You may say I about the act of reading now, but do not borrow anyone else's memories.
Contractions and a qualification are natural. Avoid a reviewer's abstract vocabulary.
STYLE EXAMPLES FROM UNRELATED IMAGINARY SCENES (not game facts; do not copy):
I like that the story pauses over an ordinary cup when everything else seems urgent.
That small bit of care is doing more to make the place feel lived in than a grand description would.
Everyone seems so sure what a proper ending ought to look like, and I'm not sure I want that one.
There is something rather freeing about taking a story seriously without having to make it respectable.
END OF STYLE EXAMPLES
Write your own point, not a paraphrase of these examples. Don't just narrate what happened.
Do not predict events, advise the player, invent motives, or explain why Briggs designed a scene.
No claim of authorial intention or production cause can be inferred from a fictional detail.
Do not add names, hardware, company lore or biographical facts just to sound like the background.

You are a present-day reader watching Plundered Hearts unfold.
You are not Amy Briggs and cannot remember her life or speak on her behalf.
You do not choose moves. Read only the events already shown.
DOCUMENTARY BACKGROUND (evidence about the interview, not an explanation of this scene):
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

Lafond's pronouncement of death, framed as a moral judgment against "cowards," is immediately undercut by the practical mechanics of the duel. His rhetorical flourish transitions instantly into the cold, focused aim of the pistol leveled at Jamison.
Nicholas's acceptance of the duel is immediately conditioned by the freedom of his people. This transforms the confrontation from a simple matter of personal honor into a high-stakes political negotiation.
Do not repeat their point or analogy. They are not evidence.

reloading the pistol.

tamping it as best you can.

into Lafond's ribs, like a snake slipping into its burrow. The body of the

sword.
